section.title: Renewed Praise of the Bride
section.sectionRationale: After the night of seeking, the bridegroom returns to praise. He calls his bride as beautiful as Tirzah, as lovely as Jerusalem, and overwhelming as an army with banners. Among all the queens and concubines she is his one dove, his perfect one, unique. The friends ask, who is this who shines like the dawn, and the movement ends with the call, come back, O Shulammite, that we may gaze upon you.
section.thesis: The bridegroom renews his praise of the bride as uniquely beautiful and wholly his own, one dove among all the rest, and both friends and beloved marvel at her radiance as she shines like the dawn.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the bridegroom overcome by his darling's beauty, more overwhelming than an army; his one dove, unique among all the queens, whom even they call blessed; and the wondering question, who is this who shines like the dawn, with the call for the Shulammite to return.

units.label: As beautiful as Tirzah, overwhelming as an army

verses.text: You are as beautiful, my {{raya|darling}}, as Tirzah, as lovely as Jerusalem, as majestic as troops with banners.
Turn your eyes away from me, for they have overcome me. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of sheep coming up from the washing; each has its twin, and not one of them is lost.
Your brow behind your veil is like a slice of pomegranate.

units.label: My dove, my perfect one, is unique

verses.text: There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number,
but my dove, my {{tammah|perfect one}}, is unique, the favorite of the mother who bore her. The maidens see her and call her blessed; the queens and concubines sing her praises.

units.label: Who is this who shines like the dawn

verses.text: Who is this who shines like the dawn, as fair as the moon, as bright as the sun, as majestic as the stars in procession?
I went down to the walnut grove to see the blossoms of the valley, to see if the vines were budding or the pomegranates were in bloom.
Before I realized it, my desire had set me among the royal chariots of my people.
Come back, come back, O {{shulammite|Shulammite}}! Come back, come back, that we may gaze upon you. Why do you look at the Shulammite, as on the dance of Mahanaim?

raya.gloss: My darling, literally my companion or dear friend, the bridegroom's recurring name for the bride. Here it opens his renewed praise, you are as beautiful, my darling, as Tirzah.

tammah.gloss: My perfect one, my flawless one. The bridegroom calls the bride his dove, his perfect one, unique among all the queens and maidens; the word carries wholeness and integrity, one wholly his and without flaw in his eyes.

shulammite.gloss: The Shulammite, the only proper name given the bride in the Song. It may point to her home town or echo the word for peace, shalom; the friends call her back so they may gaze upon her radiance.

basic.context: After the anguish of the night search, the bridegroom returns with fresh praise. He tells his bride she is as beautiful as the loveliest cities, Tirzah and Jerusalem, and as overwhelming as an army with banners; her gaze undoes him. Among all the queens and concubines of a royal court she stands out as his one dove, his perfect one, unique, and even they call her blessed. Then a wondering voice asks, who is this who shines like the dawn, and the movement closes with the cry, come back, O Shulammite, that we may gaze upon you.
basic.hermeneutics: On the plain level this is a husband's renewed delight in his wife after conflict and separation, love that returns to praise rather than blame. The imagery is poetic: cities, armies, sun and moon, all to say she is beautiful, singular, and dazzling. Within the whole Bible, the church has heard here the beauty the Lord sees in His people, one bride singled out from among the many, radiant not by her own glory but by His.
basic.originalLanguages: The man calls the bride raya, my darling, his companion, and then tammah, my perfect one, his dove, unique among all the rest. She is given the name Shulammite, the only name she bears in the Song, perhaps tied to peace, shalom. The friends ask who is this who shines like the dawn, a question of wonder at her borrowed radiance.
basic.typology: The one dove singled out from among the many queens pictures the church chosen and set apart, the one the Lord calls unique and blessed. The bride who shines like the dawn foreshadows the people who reflect the glory of their Lord, fair as the moon and bright as the sun.
basic.christ: The bridegroom's renewed praise after failure pictures the love of Christ that returns to His people not with reproach but with delight, calling them beautiful and unique still. The bride who shines like the dawn is the church made radiant with a borrowed light, reflecting the glory of the Lord who never turns His love away.
basic.god: God does not love His people grudgingly or for a season; He delights in them, calls them unique among all the world, and returns to praise even after they have failed Him. His steadfast love makes the beloved radiant, so that she shines with a light that is really His.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 5:27, the church presented in splendor, without spot. Zephaniah 3:17, the LORD will rejoice over you with singing. 2 Corinthians 3:18, beholding His glory, we are transformed into the same image. Matthew 13:45 to 46, the one pearl of great price.
basic.oneStory: After the night of failure and searching, love returns to praise: the bridegroom names his bride unique and radiant, one dove among all the rest. It pictures the unwavering delight of Christ in His church, whom He makes to shine with His own glory.

context.literary:
Song 6:4-13 is the third of the Song's great praise poems, and it is built largely from borrowed lines. Verses 5b to 7a repeat the description of hair, teeth and brow from Song 4:1 to 3 almost word for word. The repetition is deliberate. The poet does not find new words for a woman who has become familiar; he says the old words again and means them more. Love that has passed through a night of absence returns to its first language.

The unit has a clear shape. Verses 4 to 7 are the man's address, framed by the military simile of verse 4 and the veiled brow of verse 7. Verses 8 and 9 widen the lens to the whole royal court, with a graded count: sixty, eighty, then 'without number.' Verse 10 is a question from a third voice, and the same question 'Who is this?' has now been asked three times in the Song, at 3:6, here, and at 8:5. Each time it announces an arrival, and each time the answer is the bride, so the repeated question works like a refrain that tracks her progress from wilderness procession to dawn to the final climb.

Verses 11 to 13 are the hardest lines in the book to follow. The speaker changes without warning, the verbs are difficult, and the BSB footnotes admit that verse 12 could read 'among the chariots of Amminadab' and verse 13 'the dance of the two camps.' A careful reader should hold these verses loosely: the general movement, a lover's surprise at being swept off, followed by a chorus calling the bride to return so that they may look, is clear even where the details are not.
context.historical:
Tirzah is the key to the first simile. It was an old Canaanite royal town, and after the kingdom divided it served as the capital of the northern kingdom under Jeroboam, 1 Kings 14:17, until Omri moved the throne to Samaria after reigning six years in Tirzah, 1 Kings 16:23-24. Pairing it with Jerusalem sets the two royal capitals side by side, northern and southern, and the poem therefore says that she is as lovely as a kingdom's seat of power. The poem uses the beauty of a capital city, not the military or political reality, which is why the pairing is not an embarrassing reminder of the later split.

The simile of 'troops with banners' draws on the military vocabulary of Israel's camps, where each tribe stood under its own standard, Numbers 2:2. A banner meant ordered strength: an army drawn up, not a rabble. Verse 4 therefore says that her beauty is awesome in the old sense, something that makes a man step back.

Sixty queens and eighty concubines describe a royal household of the type that surrounded ancient kings. The Song's own Solomon is credited with far greater numbers, seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, 1 Kings 11:3, so the figures here are a smaller, poetic count. The point is not arithmetic. Behind it stands a world in which a king could have any number of women, and the poet uses that world as a foil: with all of them available, he declares that she is the one.
context.canonical:
The thought that one bride is singled out from a crowd of rivals runs deep in Scripture. Israel is the one people chosen from the nations, and the prophets speak of the LORD as husband and Israel as bride, Isaiah 54:5-6. Ezekiel 16:8-14 tells the story of a foundling raised, clothed and crowned, whose beauty 'was perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you.' Her radiance is a gift, a point the Song also hints at when its chorus compares her to heavenly lights rather than to anything she made.

Psalm 45:9-15 shows a royal wedding where the queen stands at the king's right hand among the daughters of kings, and the bride is led in with joy. The New Testament picks up the picture of a bride made ready, Revelation 19:7-9, and of the holy city 'shining with the glory of God,' Revelation 21:10-11, where the city has no need of sun or moon because 'the Lamb is its lamp,' Revelation 21:23. The Song's question 'Who is this who shines like the dawn?' finds its fullest answer there.

Isaiah 62:3-5 supplies the nearest parallel in tone: the forsaken are renamed, and 'as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.' The praise of a husband who sees only beauty in the one he loves is the human mirror of that promise.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet is answering a question left open by the night of chapter 5: after the wound of the closed door and the lost beloved, has anything changed between them? The answer of 6:4 to 9 is that nothing has been lost. The bridegroom does not scold her for her earlier delay or ask for an explanation. He speaks in the old words, and says that her eyes overwhelm him.

The poet also intends to set this love against the culture of the palace. Sixty queens and eighty concubines were the normal furniture of a king's world. Against that, the Song sets a plain statement that she is 'unique,' and the court itself agrees, calling her blessed and singing her praises. Hearers are meant to see that real love is exclusive and is not made smaller by comparison.

Finally he intends the wondering question of verse 10 to teach the reader how to look at the beloved: with astonishment, as at a sunrise. A husband who has learned to say 'Who is this?' about his own wife has kept his eyes open.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes a husband's praise and a chorus's astonishment. It does not command a particular form of speech, and it would be wrong to treat the list of body images, hair like goats or teeth like sheep, as a template that every husband must copy. Those images belonged to a particular culture's vocabulary of beauty, and they are meant to be read as warm, not clinical.

What does carry forward is the pattern of the speech. The man praises after an estrangement, not instead of dealing with it, and his praise is exclusive, prizing one woman over every other. Proverbs 31:28 shows the same pattern in a household: her children call her blessed, and her husband praises her as well. Believers are invited to learn to praise aloud, to return to old words of love rather than let them go stale, and to refuse the comparison with others that so often undermines a marriage.

The verses about the royal harem are descriptive, not an endorsement. Scripture records the practice of multiple wives without commending it, 1 Kings 11:3.

debates.question: Who is the Shulammite, and what is the dance of Mahanaim?

views.label: A title for the bride, perhaps tied to Solomon's name or to peace
views.case: The name appears only here in the Song, in verse 13. Because the Hebrew shares its consonants with the roots behind 'Solomon' and 'peace,' some read it as the feminine counterpart to the king's name, so that the lovers carry matching names. On this view 'Mahanaim' is simply a place known for dancing, and the BSB footnote 'the dance of the two camps' reads the same word as a description of a dance with two groups.

views.label: A woman from Shunem
views.case: Others hear a place name and think of Shunem in the north, so that the bride is the Shunammite, in the way that Abishag is called in 1 Kings 1:3. This fits the poem's northern flavour, with Tirzah, Gilead and Carmel, and treats the dance as a famous folk dance of the region of Mahanaim, where Jacob once met the angels and called the place 'the camp of God,' Genesis 32:1-2.

views.label: A deliberately open, symbolic figure
views.case: A few readers take the bride as a type rather than a biography, and say the poet leaves her name uncertain so that the dance of two camps can stand for the meeting of two companies, perhaps the two groups of friends, perhaps heaven and earth.

debates.bearing: The grammar of the name and the point of the dance remain uncertain, and nothing in the teaching of the passage rests on them. What the text plainly says is that the bride is called back so that others may gaze, and that she is treated as the delight of a community. A reader can hold the details loosely and still follow the poem.

debates.question: Who speaks in verses 11 and 12, and what is the bridegroom doing?

views.label: The bridegroom, surprised by love
views.case: On this reading the man went down to the walnut grove to look at the spring growth, and before he knew it his desire put him among the royal chariots, meaning that he was swept into the splendour of the bride and her retinue. It fits the surprise he has just voiced in verse 5, where her eyes overcame him.

views.label: The bride, describing her own excursion
views.case: Others hear the bride, who went to the grove to see whether the vines had budded and found herself carried along in an unexpected royal procession. The verb forms are ambiguous, and verse 13 can then be the court telling her to turn back.

views.label: A deliberately broken, dreamlike passage
views.case: Some think the text is damaged or intentionally elusive, a gap between the poems. The footnote 'among the chariots of Amminadab' shows that translators disagree even on whether a proper name is hiding in the verse.

debates.bearing: Whichever speaker is chosen, the same truth stands: love sometimes carries people beyond their plans. The safest course is to refuse to build any doctrine on verse 12 and to rest on the clear statements of verses 8 to 10.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 4 holds a word that English softens. 'Majestic' translates a rare adjective whose sense is closer to 'awe-inspiring' or 'terrible,' and the same word recurs in verse 10. Read together, the two verses frame the whole poem with fear mixed with delight. The simile 'troops with banners' uses a participle built on the root behind degel, 'banner,' the same root as the 'banner over me is love' of Song 2:4. There the banner announces love's claim; here it describes the beloved as an army drawn up for battle. The Hebrew thought is that beauty can be an irresistible force.

The man says of her eyes in verse 5, 'they have overcome me.' The BSB renders it 'overcome,' and the sense is that her gaze has overpowered him. It is a surprising thing for a man to say of himself, and it explains why he asks her to turn her eyes away.

Verse 9 uses 'unique,' and the Hebrew is the ordinary word for 'one,' in its feminine form, so that she is, literally, 'one.' The word does the work of both uniqueness and wholeness. The praise 'my perfect one' repeats tammati from Song 5:2, and the word comes from a root for wholeness or integrity, the same family used of a blameless person in the Psalms. The poet also says she is the favourite of her mother, using the language of the family circle to stress belonging.

The maidens 'call her blessed,' and the verb is the one in Proverbs 31:28, where children call the capable wife blessed. The word is about praise that is spoken out, not just felt. That the queens and concubines, who might have been rivals, join the chorus is part of the poem's point.

In verse 10 the heavenly lights have their own Hebrew words. The 'dawn' is shachar, the moon is called the 'white one,' and the sun the 'hot one.' So the question compares her to the cool brightness of the moon and the burning brightness of the sun. 'Stars in procession' renders the same battle word again, so that even the heavens are drawn up with banners.

Finally, verse 13 repeats 'Come back' four times, and the verb shuv is the ordinary word for turning or returning. It is the same verb the bride herself used when she bade her beloved 'turn' in Song 2:17. The call to return is an invitation of the community to a woman who had been away, and it reverses the departure of chapter 5.

typology.type: The one dove among sixty queens, Song 6:8-9
typology.fulfillment: The picture of one chosen from among a multitude corresponds to God's choice of Israel from all nations and, in the New Testament, of the church. Paul wrote to the Corinthians that he had promised them 'to one husband,' to present them as a pure virgin to Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:2. The escalation lies in the bridegroom: in Christ the choice is made at the price of His life, Ephesians 5:25. The type falls short because the Song's lover is one person among many courts, while Christ's bride is a multitude drawn from every nation, Revelation 7:9, who are nonetheless one body.

typology.type: Beauty that shines like the dawn, Song 6:10
typology.fulfillment: The bride's brightness is compared to heavenly lights that are not her own, and that matches the Bible's picture of a people who shine with a given glory. Ezekiel 16:14 says her beauty was perfect 'in the splendor I bestowed on you,' and Paul writes that those who behold the Lord's glory are being transformed into His image, 2 Corinthians 3:18. In Revelation the bride is the city shining with God's glory, whose lamp is the Lamb, Revelation 21:11 and 21:23. The type falls short because the lights of verse 10 are only similes, while the glory of the new Jerusalem is real and everlasting.

typology.type: The renewed praise after estrangement, Song 6:4-5
typology.fulfillment: After the night of chapter 5 the bridegroom does not rehearse her failure but speaks his old praise again. Hosea 2:14-16 shows the LORD allure the wife who wandered, speak tenderly to her, and give back what she lost, until she calls Him 'my Husband.' Isaiah 54:6 says the LORD has called her back 'like a wife deserted.' The fulfilment is Christ, who restored Peter after denial with a question of love, John 21:15-17. The type falls short because a human husband's forgiveness is always partial, while the grace of Christ cleanses fully, Ephesians 5:26-27.

typology.type: Called back so that others may gaze, Song 6:13
typology.fulfillment: The chorus's cry 'Come back' so that they may look pictures the church as something the watching world and the heavenly host are meant to see. Paul says that through the church the manifold wisdom of God is made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms, Ephesians 3:10, and Jesus tells His disciples that people will see their good works and glorify the Father, Matthew 5:16. The image is only a suggestion and the Song does not say why the chorus wishes to gaze, so the link should be held lightly.

study.christ:
The passage does not name Christ, and a faithful reading begins with the husband and wife. But the New Testament teaches that marriage is a picture of Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32, and under that light the poem's movements gain a second depth.

First, the bridegroom's praise returns after failure. In the Song the night of chapter 5 was a night of delay and a closed door, and yet here nothing is said of it. Christ treats His people the same way. After Peter's denial, the risen Lord asks only 'Do you love Me?' and gives him work to do, John 21:15-17. The disciples had scattered and the Lord's first words to them were 'Peace be with you,' John 20:19. The love of verse 4 is a love that has seen the failure and still names her beautiful.

Second, the one dove 'unique' among the many fits the way Christ speaks of His people. He calls them 'My sheep,' knows them by name, John 10:3, and says of those given to Him that none will be lost, John 6:39. Where the king of the palace has sixty queens, Christ has one bride, 2 Corinthians 11:2, made of many members.

Third, the beauty is a gift. The bride shines like the dawn, but the images are heavenly lights she borrows. Ephesians 5:26-27 says that Christ washes the church so that He might present her to Himself 'a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle.' She is radiant because He has made her so. When the Song's chorus asks 'Who is this?' the wondering answer is that the glory is not her own. Revelation 21:23 completes the thought: the city shines because 'the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp.'

Fourth, the bridegroom is overcome by her eyes. In an astonishing statement of divine delight, Zephaniah 3:17 says that the LORD 'will rejoice over you with singing.' The Christ of the Gospels is the one in whom this rejoicing is seen: He is moved with compassion, weeps at a tomb, and for the joy set before Him endures a cross, Hebrews 12:2. The joy He has in His people is not a metaphor for indifference.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The body images of verses 5 to 7, hair, teeth and brow, are not codes for church offices or doctrines, and the early practice of assigning each one a spiritual meaning goes beyond what the text supports. The legitimate link is at the level of the whole scene: a bridegroom who delights in one bride above all rivals, and renews that delight after she has failed him, tells the truth about the love of Christ.
study.god:
This passage shows a love that is exclusive, unhurried and glad, and it lets us say several things about the God whose love marriage is made to picture.

First, God's love is particular. Verse 9 does not say that the bride is one among many equally treasured. It says she is unique. Scripture speaks of God's love in the same way: He set His love on Israel not because they were many, Deuteronomy 7:7, and the Son is said to give Himself for 'her,' the church, Ephesians 5:25. God does not love in general only; He knows the ones He loves.

Second, His love returns. The bridegroom speaks his earlier words again, and the Lord speaks of a love that comes back to the wandering, Hosea 2:14-16 and Jeremiah 31:3, 'I have loved you with an everlasting love.' Faithfulness, in the Bible, is not the absence of failure on the beloved's side but the refusal of the lover to let it have the last word.

Third, God delights. The text does not treat beauty as a distraction. The bridegroom enjoys his bride's beauty, and Zephaniah 3:17 uses the language of singing for God's own gladness. A God who simply tolerated His people would not be the God of the Bible. This is also a corrective for those who imagine God mainly as a distant judge: Isaiah 62:5 says that the LORD will rejoice over His people as a bridegroom over his bride.

Fourth, God is the source of the glory He praises. The comparison to dawn, moon and sun makes the same point as Genesis 1: the lights in the sky are made things, and the radiance of the bride is made radiance. God gives the beauty and then speaks over it. Ezekiel 16:14 holds both halves: 'Your fame spread among the nations on account of your beauty, for it was perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you.'

Fifth, God is holy and awesome. The phrase 'majestic as troops with banners' says that love is not tame. The beauty of the beloved is dangerous in the best sense, and the same is true of the God whose love is fierce, which the Song will say outright in 8:6.

For worship, the passage teaches us to answer the Lord's praise of His people with wonder, and to take the Song's chorus question as our own. 'Who is this?' is the question angels ask of the ones He has redeemed, and the right reply is to give Him the glory.

crossReferences.note: The source of the repeated lines in 6:5-7. Hair like goats, teeth like shorn sheep, brow behind the veil: the lover says again what he said on the wedding day. Setting the passages side by side shows that his praise has not faded. It has survived the night of chapter 5.

The first 'Who is this?' of the Song asks about a procession coming up from the wilderness. In 6:10 the same question is turned to the bride, now as bright as the dawn. The refrain follows her progress through the Song, and its last use at 8:5 finds her leaning on her beloved.

Solomon is said to have seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and the text adds that they turned his heart away. Against that background, the poet's 'sixty queens and eighty concubines' with one dove singled out becomes a quiet protest. Love that is shared among many is a different thing from the love of verse 9.

Tirzah was the capital of the northern kingdom until Omri moved the throne. The poet's choice of Tirzah beside Jerusalem is probably a choice of the best-loved royal cities, not a commentary on later history, but it reminds the reader that cities of beauty were also centres of rule and ambition.

The children call the capable wife blessed, and her husband adds his praise: 'you surpass them all!' It is the closest wisdom parallel to Song 6:9, with the same shape of a household and a court praising one woman and the husband's voice joining them.

The LORD describes how He covered, washed and adorned the foundling who became Jerusalem, and her beauty was 'perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you.' It shows that the beauty praised in a bride can be a given beauty, which is how the church has read the dawn imagery of verse 10.

The forsaken are given a new name and God declares that as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride so He will rejoice over His people. It is the prophetic counterpart of the bridegroom's renewed praise, and it makes the Song's delight a picture of God's.

Christ gave Himself up for the church to present her to Himself without stain or wrinkle. Where the Song's bride is praised as already fair, Paul explains how the beauty comes about: by the washing of the Lord. The two texts together say that He both makes and loves the bride.

The angel shows John the bride, the wife of the Lamb, and she appears as the holy city shining with the glory of God. The Song's question about the one who shines like the dawn is answered by the city whose light is the Lamb. The poem's language of brightness reaches its goal here.

The LORD is in your midst and rejoices over you with singing. The bridegroom's overwhelmed delight in verses 4 and 5 is a faint human echo of this, a statement that God's gladness over His people is real and expressed.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a man and a woman in a garden, and the first words of a husband in Scripture are a cry of delight over his wife, Genesis 2:23. The fall broke that unashamed gladness, and much of the rest of the story is the long labour of restoring it. The Song's praise poems are a kind of Eden regained in miniature. A man looks at a woman and says what he sees, with no fear and no deceit. That is why the poem of 6:4 to 13 does not feel like an interruption of the story but a signpost within it.

The story of Israel turns on the question of whether the people will be faithful to the one who chose them. The prophets use the language of marriage again and again: the husband loves, the bride strays, the husband calls her back, Isaiah 54:5-6 and Hosea 2:14-16. The Song's scene of praise after estrangement answers in advance the fear that the answer must be rejection. It looks like the Hosea scene seen from the side of delight.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, who is called the bridegroom, Matthew 9:15 and John 3:29. He gave Himself for His bride, cleansing her, and presents her to Himself in splendour, Ephesians 5:25-27. Between His giving and His presenting lies the time in which we live, in which the bride is still being made ready, Revelation 19:7. The lines of verse 10 are therefore something like a preview: a company still on its way, yet already praised.

The story ends in a city. The woman the Song asks about is shown to John as the holy city, shining with the glory of God, her lamp the Lamb, Revelation 21:9-11 and 21:23. Every rival is gone, every court of queens is finished, and the multitude of the redeemed stand as one bride. The wondering question, 'Who is this who shines like the dawn?', is answered by the God who set His love on her and who now, at last, shines on her face to face.

quiz.q: To what does the bridegroom compare the bride's beauty in 6:4?

options.text: To the lovely cities Tirzah and Jerusalem, and to an army with banners.
options.note: He likens her to the most beautiful cities and to dazzling, ordered might.

options.text: To a ruined and abandoned town.
options.note: He does compare her to a city, but to the loveliest cities, Tirzah and Jerusalem, not to a ruined and abandoned town.

options.text: To an ordinary field.
options.note: He does draw on the created world for his images, but here he reaches for the most striking, cities and an army with banners, not an ordinary field.

options.text: To a fading flower.
options.note: His praise is of overwhelming beauty, not decline.

quiz.q: How does the bridegroom set the bride apart from all the queens and maidens in 6:9?

options.text: She is his one dove, his perfect one, unique, and even they call her blessed.
options.note: She is singled out as unique among all the rest.

options.text: She is merely one of many equals.
options.note: She is truly set among the many queens and maidens, but he singles her out as his one perfect dove, unique, not one equal among them.

options.text: She is the least among them.
options.note: She is prized above all, his one perfect dove.

options.text: She is admired only for a moment.
options.note: She is indeed admired, but his delight in her is settled and lasting, and even the queens call her blessed, not admired only for a moment.

quiz.q: What wondering question do the friends ask in 6:10?

options.text: Who is this who shines like the dawn, fair as the moon and bright as the sun?
options.note: They marvel at her radiance, a light she reflects rather than owns.

options.text: Who is this who hides in the dark?
options.note: It echoes their wondering, who is this, but they marvel that she shines like the dawn, not that she hides in the dark.

options.text: Why is this woman so plain?
options.note: The wonder is at her dazzling beauty, not plainness.

options.text: Where has this stranger come from?
options.note: It rightly echoes their wondering, who is this, but their marvel is at her radiance, shining like the dawn, not merely at where she came from.

quiz.q: How does the bridegroom's renewed praise picture the love of Christ?

options.text: He returns after the night of failure to delight in his bride, not to reproach her.
options.note: Christ's love restores His failing people and delights in them still.

options.text: He waits until she has made herself perfect before loving her again.
options.note: He does return to her after her failure in the night, but not because she has first made herself perfect; he praises her freely, and her radiance is borrowed, reflected light.

options.text: He abandons her for her failure in the night.
options.note: The opposite: he returns with praise and restoration.

options.text: He loves her only while she is useful.
options.note: His love does bless and honor her, but it is settled love that calls her unique and blessed, not love that lasts only while she is useful.

quiz.q: What does the bride shining like the dawn picture in the whole Bible?

options.text: The church made radiant with the reflected glory of her Lord.
options.note: She shines with borrowed light, as believers are transformed beholding His glory.

options.text: That believers glow by their own goodness.
options.note: Believers do truly shine, but with light reflected from their Lord, not with a glow of their own goodness.

options.text: That God's people have no glory at all.
options.note: Her glory is indeed not her own, but she truly does shine, fair as the moon and bright as the sun, with His borrowed light, so it is not that she has no glory at all.

options.text: That beauty is worthless to God.
options.note: The passage celebrates the beauty God gives His beloved.

questions: The bridegroom returns after the night of failure with praise, not blame. How does it move you that Christ comes back to His failing people to delight in them rather than reproach them?
Among all the queens the bride is his one dove, unique. Have you let yourself believe that the Lord prizes you as singular and set apart, not lost in a crowd?
Who is this who shines like the dawn? The bride's radiance is borrowed from her beloved. Where might you be trying to shine by your own light instead of reflecting His?
The bridegroom says her eyes overwhelm him. How does knowing that the Lord delights in His people change the way you come to Him?
The queens and maidens end up singing her praises. How can you speak well of the beauty God has worked in someone else this week, rather than envying it?

translationNotes.note: Tirzah and Jerusalem were prized royal cities; troops with banners renders an image of ordered, dazzling might, sometimes translated an army with banners.
This is one of the most difficult verses in the Song; the sense of my desire had set me among the royal chariots is uncertain, and a footnote offers among the chariots of Amminadab.
Shulammite is the only proper name given the bride, perhaps tied to shalom, peace; the dance of Mahanaim, or dance of the two camps, remains debated.
